summary_html: Findings by **federal/state oversight** (CFSR reviews, OIG audits, child-fatality commissions) can initiate investigations or corrective actions that open CPS involvement.
authority_html:
- **Protect Our Kids Act (PL 112-275)** — national commission on child abuse/neglect fatalities  
- **Child & Family Services Reviews (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal monitoring of state systems  
- **Inspector General Act (5 U.S.C. App.)** — OIG oversight of HHS/ACF and grantees

primary_citations.citation_text: Montana - Title 41, Chapter 3 (Child Abuse and Neglect – mandatory reporting and protective services)

regulations_applicable.title: Department 37 - PUBLIC HEALTH AND HUMAN SERVICES

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Mercer v. Montana Department of Public Health & Human Services
key_cases.holding: A mandatory preliminary injunction requiring DPHHS to disclose child abuse and neglect case records to a state legislator conducting a statutory review under § 41-3-205(4) was affirmed; the legislator had an absolute statutory right to the described records subject only to the statute's own limits, and a stipulation barring further disclosure minimized any harm to the Department.
key_cases.relevance: It is the Montana Supreme Court's enforcement of legislative oversight over DPHHS child-protection files and the concrete remedy — mandatory injunction — when the agency withholds them.
key_cases.quote: This statute requires that child abuse and neglect “case records” be kept confidential but also provides for disclosure of such records upon satisfaction of statutory criteria

key_cases.holding: Any Montana citizen has standing under Article II, Section 9 to seek judicial relief for a denial of access to the documents of any Montana public body, without needing a nexus to or residence in that body's jurisdiction; the individual-privacy limitation and any confidentiality provisions remain to be applied on remand.
key_cases.relevance: It gives any citizen — not just a party or resident — standing to compel production of the records that make outside oversight of a public agency possible.
key_cases.quote: We hold Article II, Section 9 grants a right to judicial relief to a Montana citizen alleging denial of access to a document of a Montana public body.

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The 'reasonable efforts' clause of the Adoption Assistance and Child Welfare Act, 42 U.S.C. § 671(a)(15), does not create a right enforceable by private plaintiffs under § 1983, nor an implied private right of action; compliance is enforced by the Secretary through the plan-approval and funding process.
key_cases.relevance: It explains why federal child-welfare compliance is policed through administrative review and funding rather than private litigation, making oversight findings the practical remedy.
key_cases.quote: the “reasonable efforts” language does not unambiguously confer an enforceable right upon the Act's beneficiaries

key_cases.holding: Reversed and remanded: a county resident has standing to pursue right-to-know and right-of-participation claims without alleging an injury distinguishable from that of the public generally, because the personal stake those provisions require is the opportunity to observe and participate in the public body's decision-making, and Fleenor is overruled to the extent it held otherwise.
key_cases.relevance: It is the standing decision Shockley v. Cascade County builds on, and it removes the 'injury distinguishable from the public generally' barrier that agencies had used to defeat citizen oversight suits.
key_cases.quote: we hold that Schoof has standing to pursue further discovery on his claims, and overrule Fleenor to the extent that it is inconsistent with this opinion

search_keywords: Montana Department of Public Health and Human Services

state_agency.name: Montana Department of Public Health and Human Services, Child and Family Services Division

mandatory_reporters: Physicians, residents, interns, and hospital staff engaged in the admission, examination, care, or treatment of persons — Mont. Code Ann. § 41-3-201(2)(a)
Nurses, osteopaths, chiropractors, podiatrists, medical examiners, coroners, dentists, optometrists, and any other health or mental health professionals — Mont. Code Ann. § 41-3-201(2)(b)
School teachers, other school officials, and employees who work during regular school hours — Mont. Code Ann. § 41-3-201(2)(d)

Social workers licensed pursuant to Title 37, child protection investigators, child reunification specialists, operators or employees of any registered or licensed day-care or substitute care facility, staff of a resource and referral grant program organized under § 52-2-711 or of a child and adult food care program, and operators or employees of a child-care facility — Mont. Code Ann. § 41-3-201(2)(e)
Foster care, residential, and institutional workers — Mont. Code Ann. § 41-3-201(2)(f)
Peace officers and other law enforcement officials — Mont. Code Ann. § 41-3-201(2)(g)
Members of the clergy, subject to the confessional and canon-law exceptions — Mont. Code Ann. § 41-3-201(2)(h), (6)(b)–(c)
Guardians ad litem and court-appointed advocates authorized to investigate a report of alleged abuse or neglect — Mont. Code Ann. § 41-3-201(2)(i)
Employees of entities that contract with the department to provide direct services to children — Mont. Code Ann. § 41-3-201(2)(j)
Department employees while in the conduct of their duties — Mont. Code Ann. § 41-3-201(2)(k)

Added duty: a professional listed in § 41-3-201(2)(a) or (2)(b) who is involved in the delivery or care of an infant must report any infant known to the professional to be affected by a dangerous drug, as defined in § 50-32-101 — Mont. Code Ann. § 41-3-201(3)
reporting_details: Montana is not a universal-reporter state: only the professionals and officials listed in Mont. Code Ann. § 41-3-201(2) must report promptly to the department when, in their professional or official capacity, they know or have reasonable cause to suspect a child is abused or neglected, while § 41-3-201(4) allows any other person to report voluntarily.

timeline_requirements.requirement_name: Written safety and risk assessment furnished
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Statute states no penalty; within 60 days the child protection investigator must furnish the written safety and risk assessment to the department and, on request, to the family (Mont. Code Ann. § 41-3-202(6))
